{{RunningHeader|three|6308|three-quarter}}{{smaller|'''The three R's.''' See ''R.''—'''The Three Sisters.''' See ''sister.''—'''Three-armed cross,''' a figure composed of three lines parting from a common center, either in the form of a Y (see ''Y-cross''), or composed of three hooks as if a figure in revolution, or of three arms broken at an angle, and bending all in the same direction. See ''triskele.''—'''Three-card monte.''' See ''monte.''—'''Three-cylinder steam-engine,''' a triple expansion-cylinder steam-engine. See ''steam-engine.''—'''Three-day fever,''' dengue.—'''Three-em brace,''' in ''printing,'' a brace three ems wide.—'''Three estates.''' See ''estate,'' 9.—'''Three-field system.''' See ''field.''—'''Three hours.''' See ''hour.''—'''Three kings of Cologne.''' See ''king''1.—'''Three-line letter,''' in ''printing,'' an initial letter which is the height of three lines of the body of the type of the text in which it is used.—'''Three-mile limit, zone,''' or '''belt.''' See ''mile.''—'''Three-million bill.''' See ''million''1.—'''Three sheets in the wind.''' See ''a sheet in the wind,'' under ''sheet''1.—'''Three thirds†, three threads†,''' a mixture of three malt liquors, formerly in demand, as equal parts of ale, beer, and twopenny. Compare ''entire'' and ''porter''3.}} {{smaller block|Ezekiel Driver, of Puddle-dock, carman, having disorder'd his pia mater with too plentiful a morning's draught of ''three-threads'' and old Pharaoh, had the misfortune to have his cart run over him. {{right|''Tom Brown,'' Works, II. 286. (''Davies.'')}}}} {{smaller|'''Three times three,''' three cheers thrice repeated.}} {{smaller block|Again the feast, the speech, the glee, . . . The crowning cup, the ''three-times-three.'' {{right|''Tennyson,'' In Memoriam, Conclusion.}}}} {{smaller block|Before I sit down I must give you a toast to be drunk with ''three-times-three'' and all the honours. {{right|''T. Hughes,'' Tom Brown at Rugby, i. 6.}}}} {{smaller|'''Three trees†,''' the gallows, formed by a transverse beam on two uprights.}} {{smaller block|For commonly such knaues as these Doe end their lyves vpon ''three trees.'' {{right|''Breton,'' Toyes of an Idle Head, p. 28. (''Davies.'')}}}} '''II.''' ''n.'' 1. A number the sum of two and one. {{smaller block|My face so thin That in my ear I durst not stick a rose, Lest men should say, "Look, where ''three-farthings'' goes!" {{right|''Shak.,'' K. John, i. 1. 143.}}}} {{smaller block|He values me at a crack'd ''three-farthings,'' for aught I see. {{right|''B. Jonson,'' Every Man in his Humour, ii. 1.}}}} '''threefold''' (thrē′fōld), ''a.'' and ''n.'' [< ME. ''threfold, threovold, threfald,'' < AS. ''thrīfeald, thriefeald, thriefald, threófeald'' (= OFries. ''thrifald'' = MLG. ''drēvalt, drivolt'' = OHG. ''drifalt,'' MHG. ''drivalt'' = Icel. ''threfaldr;'' also, with added adj. termination, = D. ''drievoudig'' = OHG. ''drifalt,'' MHG. ''drivalt, drivaltec,'' G. ''dreifältig'' = Sw. ''trefaldig'' = Dan. ''trefoldig''), < ''threó,'' three, + ''-feald,'' E. ''-fold.''] '''I.''' ''a.'' Consisting of three in one, or one thrice repeated; multiplied by three; triple: as, ''threefold'' justice. {{smaller block|A ''threefold'' cord is not quickly broken. Eccles. iv. 12.}} '''II.''' ''n.'' The bog-bean, ''Menyanthes trifoliata.'' '''threefold''' (thrē′fōld), ''adv.'' In a threefold manner; trebly; thrice: often used in an intensive way, with the sense of 'much' or 'greatly.' {{smaller block|Alas, you three, on me, ''threefold'' distress'd, Pour all your tears! {{right|''Shak.,'' Rich. III., ii. 2. 86.}}}} '''Thick and threefold.''' See ''thick.'' '''three-foot''' (thrē′fu̇t), ''a.'' [< ME. *''threfote,'' < AS. ''thriefēt, thrȳfēt, thrȳfēte,'' three-foot; as ''three'' + ''foot.'' Cf. ''tripod.''] 1. Measuring three feet: as, a ''three-foot'' rule.—2. Having three feet; three-footed. {{smaller block|When on my ''three-foot'' stool I sit. {{right|''Shak.,'' Cymbeline, iii. 3. 89.}}}} '''three-footed''' (thrē′fu̇t″ed), ''a.'' [< ME. *''threfoted,'' < AS. ''thrȳfōtad,'' three-footed; as ''three'' + ''foot'' —2. A symbol representing three units, as 3, III, or iii.—3. A playing-card bearing three spots or pips.—'''Inverse rule of three.''' {{smaller|See ''inverse.''}}—'''Rule of three.''' {{smaller|See ''rule''1.}} '''three-aged''' (thrē′ājd), ''a.'' Living during three generations. [Rare.] {{smaller block|Great Atreus' sons, Tydides fixt above, With ''three-aged'' Nestor. {{right|''Creech'', tr. of Manilius.}}}} '''three-awned''' (thrē′ând), ''a.'' Having three awns.—'''Three-awned grass,''' {{smaller|an American grass, ''Aristida purpurascens;'' also, ''A. purpurea,'' purple three-awned grass. The latter is of some consequence as wild feed in the West. Also ''beard-grass.''}} '''three-bearded''' (thrē′bēr″ded), ''a.'' Having three barbels: as, the ''three-bearded'' rockling, cod, or gade (a fish, ''Motella vulgaris''). '''three-birds''' (thrē′bėrds), ''n.'' A species of toad-flax, ''Linaria triornithophora'' (see ''toad-flax''); also, ''Pogonia pendula.'' See ''Pogonia.'' '''three-bodied''' (thrē′bod″id), ''a.'' Having three bodies. [Rare.] {{smaller block|I Caia Manlia, daughter to Caius Manlius, doe carie with me mine owne present, for I giue my condemned soule and life to the infernall ''three-bodyed'' Pluto. {{right|''Guevara'', Letters (tr. by Hellowes, 1577), p. 336.}}}} '''three-coat''' (thrē′kōt), ''a.'' Having or requiring three coats. {{smaller|(''a'') In ''plastering'', noting work which consists of pricking-up or roughing-in, floating, and a finishing coat. (''b'') In ''house-painting'', noting work when three successive layers of paint are required.}} '''three-cornered''' (thrē′kôr″nėrd), ''a.'' 1. Having three corners or angles: as, a ''three-cornered'' hat.—2. In ''bot.'', triquetrous.—'''Three-cornered constituency,''' {{smaller|a constituency in which, while three members are returned at one election, each elector can vote for only two candidates. This enables a large minority to elect one of the three members, the majority electing}} + -''ed''2.] Having three feet: as, a ''three-footed'' stool. '''three-girred''' (thrē′gėrd), ''a.'' Surrounded with three hoops. ''Burns.'' [Scotch.] '''three-halfpence''' (thrē′hā′pe̤ns), ''n.'' An English silver coin of the value of three halfpence (3 cents), issued by Queen Elizabeth; also, a silver coin of William IV. and Queen Victoria, formerly issued for circulation in Ceylon. '''three-handed''' (thrē′han″ded), ''a.'' 1. Having three hands.—2. Done, played, etc., with three hands or by three persons: as, ''three-handed'' euchre.—'''Three-handed boring.''' {{smaller|See ''boring.''}} '''threehead†''', ''n.'' [ME. ''threhed'' (= G. ''dreiheit''); < ''three'' + ''head.''] Trinity. {{smaller block|A God and ane Lord yn ''threhed,'' And thre persons yn anehede. {{right|''Religious Pieces'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 59.}}}} '''three-hooped''' (thrē′höpt), ''a.'' Having three hoops.—'''Three-hooped pot,''' {{smaller|a quart pot. See ''hoop''1, 5.}} {{smaller block|The ''three-hooped pot'' shall have ten hoops; and I will make it felony to drink small beer. {{right|''Shak.'', 2 Hen. VI., iv. 2. 72.}}}} '''three-leaved''' (thrē′lēvd), ''a.'' In ''bot.'', having three leaves or leaflets, as many species of ''Trifolium;'' trifoliate or trifoliolate.—'''Three-leaved grass,''' {{smaller|an old book-name for clover.}}—'''Three-leaved ivy.''' {{smaller|See ''poison-ivy.''}}—'''Three-leaved nightshade,''' {{smaller|a plant of the genus ''Trillium.''}} '''three-light''' (thrē′līt), ''n.'' A chandelier or candelabrum with three lamps for candles. '''threeling''' (thrē′ling), ''n.'' Same as ''trilling'', 2. '''three-lobed''' (thrē′lōbd), ''a.'' In ''bot.'', ''zoöl.'', and ''anat.'', having three lobes; trilobate.—'''Three-lobed malope.''' {{smaller|See ''Malope.''}} the other two. There were several British constituencies of this complexion from 1867 to 1885. '''three-decker''' (thrē′dek″ėr), ''n.'' and ''a.'' '''I.''' ''n.'' A vessel of war carrying guns on three decks; formerly, a line-of-battle ship, such ships being of that description in the sailing navy and the earlier naval classification after the introduction of steam. {{smaller block|Before the gentlemen, as they stood at the door, could . . . settle the number of ''three-deckers'' now in commission, their companions were ready to proceed. {{right|''Jane Austen'', Mansfield Park, xli.}}}} '''II.''' ''a.'' Having three decks: as, a ''three-decker'' ship; hence, having three stories, tiers, or levels, as a piece of furniture or an old-fashioned pulpit. [Colloq.] {{smaller block|A ''three-decker'' sideboard, about 1700. {{right|''S. W. Ogden'', Antique Furniture, plate 32.}}}} '''three-dimensional''' (thrē′di-men″shọn-ạl), ''a.'' Same as ''tridimensional.'' '''three-man''' (thrē′man), ''a.'' Requiring three men for its use or performance. {{smaller block|Fillip me with a ''three-man'' beetle. {{right|''Shak.'', 2 Hen. IV., i. 2. 255.}}}} {{smaller|'''A three-man song†''', a song for three voices.}} {{smaller block|''Three-man-song''-men all. {{right|''Shak.'', W. T., iv. 3. 43.}}}} '''three-masted''' (thrē′mȧs″ted), ''a.'' Having three masts. '''three-master''' (thrē′mȧs″tėr), ''n.'' A three-masted vessel, especially such a schooner. '''three-nerved''' (thrē′nėrvd), ''a.'' In ''bot.'', having three nerves; triple-nerved. '''threeness''' (thrē′nes), ''n.'' [< ''three'' + ''-ness''.] The character of being three. '''three-out''' (thrē′out), ''n.'' One of three equal parts of two glasses, as of gin or ale; a third part of two portions or helpings. [Colloq., Great Britain.] {{smaller block|On one side a little crowd has collected round a couple of ladies, who, having imbibed the contents of various ''three-outs'' of gin and bitters in the course of the morning, have at length differed on some point of domestic arrangement. {{right|''Dickens'', Sketches, Scenes, v.}}}} [[File:century v08 p0112 c1f1.png|center|180px]] {{c|Piece of Three-farthings.—British Museum. (Size of the original.)}} '''threep''', ''v.'' and ''n.'' See ''threap.'' '''three-parted''' (thrē′pär″ted), ''a.'' Divided into three parts; tripartite: as, a ''three-parted'' leaf. '''threepence''' (thrē′pens, colloq. thrip′ẹns), ''n.'' '''1.''' A current English silver coin of the value of three pennies (6 cents), issued by Queen Victoria. Usually called ''threepenny-piece'' or ''threepenny''. {{smaller|A silver coin of the same denomination was coined by Edward VI. and by subsequent sovereigns till 1662, from which time till the reign of Victoria the threepence was struck only as maundy money and not for general circulation.}} [[File:century v08 p0112 c2f1.png|center|197px]] {{c|Obverse. Some ''threepence'' in the whole! {{right|''B. Jonson'', Volpone, ii. 1.}}}} '''threepenny''' (thrē′pen″i, colloq. thrip′ẹn-i), ''a.'' and ''n.'' '''I.''' ''a.'' Worth three pence only; hence, of little worth. '''II.''' ''n.'' Same as ''threepence'', 1. '''threepenny-piece''', ''n.'' Same as ''threepence'', 1. '''three-per-cents''' (thrē′pėr-sents), ''n. pl.'' Government stocks paying three per cent.; specifically, "that portion of the consolidated debt of Great Britain which originated in 1752 in consequence of some annuities granted by George I. being consolidated in one fund with a three per cent. stock formed in 1731" (''Bithell'', Counting-House Dictionary). '''three-pile†''' (thrē′pīl), ''n.'' [< ''three'' + ''pile''4, 6.] Three-piled velvet. {{smaller block|I have served Prince Florizel, and in my time wore ''three-pile.'' {{right|''Shak.'', W. T., iv. 3. 14.}}}} '''three-piled†''' (thrē′pīld), ''a.'' [< ''three'' + ''pile''4, 6, + ''-ed''2.] Having a triple pile or nap, as a costly kind of velvet (called ''three-pile''); hence, figuratively, having the qualities of three-pile. {{smaller block|''Three-piled'' hyperboles, spruce affectation. {{right|''Shak.'', L. L. L., v. 2. 407.}}}} '''three-ply''' (thrē′plī), ''a.'' Threefold; consisting of three parts or thicknesses. {{smaller|Especially—(''a'') Noting thread or cord composed of three yarns or strands. (''b'') Noting textile fabrics consisting of three webs woven one into the other: as, a ''three-ply'' carpet. (''c'') In manufactured articles, consisting of three thicknesses, as of linen in a ''three-ply'' collar or cuff.}} '''three-pound piece''' (thrē′pound pēs). An English gold coin of the value of £3 (about $14.52), {{c|Reverse.}} [[File:century v08 p0112 c2f2.png|center|197px]] {{c|Three-pound Piece.—British Museum. (Size of the original.)}} struck by Charles I. during the civil war {{sc|a. d.}} 1642–1644. Specimens weigh over 421 grains. '''three-quarter, three-quarters''' (thrē′kwâr′tėr, -tėrz), ''a.'' Involving anything three fourths of its normal size or proportions; specifically, noting a size of portraiture measuring 30 inches by 25, or a portrait delineated to the hips only.
